answer.text:
This is a common-source stage $M_{1}$ with
cascode device $M_{2}$ and active load $I_{1}$.

* $M_{1}$ is the input transconductor. Its source
is ac ground.
* $M_{2}$ is common-gate. $V_{b1}$ is ac ground.
Its source is node $X$, its drain is $v_{out}$.
* $I_{1}$ is the dc bias current and the ac load.
Let its small signal impedance to $V_{DD}$ ac
ground be $R_{1}$. For an ideal source $R_{1}=\infty$.

Assume all in saturation. Let

$$ g_{ds1}=1/r_{o1},\; g_{ds2}=1/r_{o2}$$

$M_{1}$ has $V_{SB1}=0$, no back gate.
$M_{2}$ in a common p-sub has $V_{SB2}>0$,
back gate $g_{mb2}\ne 0$ unless in own well.

DC: neglecting mismatch

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}$$

$V_{GS1}$ is set by $V_{in,DC}$ to support $I_{1}$:

$$ I_{1}\approx \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}
(V_{GS1}-V_{TH1})^{2}(1+\lambda_{1}V_{DS1}) $$

$$V_{X}=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}$$

Saturation needs:

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{X} &\ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH1}=V_{OV1} \\
V_{out} &\ge V_{X}+V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}=V_{X}+V_{OV2}\\
V_{out} &\le V_{DD}-V_{sat,I1}
\end{aligned}$$

i.e.

$$V_{b1}\ge V_{OV1}+V_{GS2}$$
$$V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{TH2}$$

With $\lambda=0$ and ideal $I_{1}$ the dc $V_{out}$
is undefined. In practice it is set by
$\lambda$ and $R_{1}$. It is a high gain node,
bias sensitive.

Small signal, low frequency.

Put $v_{in}$ at gate of $M_{1}$, $v_{x}$ at $X$,
$v_{out}$ at output. For $M_{2}$:

$$v_{gs2}=-v_{x},\quad v_{bs2}=-v_{x},\quad
v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{x}$$

Define the $M_{2}$ drain-to-source ac current:

$$i_{2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$

$$i_{2}=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})$$

For $M_{1}$:

$$i_{1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}$$

flowing from $X$ to ground.

KCL at $X$: current entering $X$ from $M_{2}$
equals current leaving $X$ into $M_{1}$:

$$i_{2}=i_{1} \tag{1}$$

KCL at output: current leaving output into $M_{2}$
plus current leaving into $R_{1}$ = 0:

$$i_{2}+v_{out}/R_{1}=0 \tag{2}$$

for open circuit load. Hence from (1)-(2):

$$\begin{aligned}
i_{2} &= -v_{out}/R_{1} \\
g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x} &= -v_{out}/R_{1}
\end{aligned}$$

and

$$-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{x})+v_{out}/R_{1}=0 $$

i.e. with $N=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}$:

$$v_{out}(g_{ds2}+1/R_{1}) = v_{x}N \tag{3}$$

Output resistance: set $v_{in}=0$, drive
output with test source. Putting $v_{in}=0$
in above gives with $B=g_{ds1}$, $C=g_{ds2}$,
$G_{1}=1/R_{1}$:

$$R_{out}=\frac{1}{G_{1}+\dfrac{BC}{B+N}}$$

i.e.

$$R_{out}=R_{1}\parallel R_{cas}$$

where $R_{cas}$ is the impedance looking into
the cascode drain:

$$R_{cas} = r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

$$\approx [1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]r_{o1}$$

This is the classic common-gate with source
resistance $r_{o1}$ result:

$$R_{d}=r_{o2}+[1+(g_{m}+g_{mb})r_{o}]R_{S}$$

For $R_{1}\to\infty$:

$$R_{out}\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

Ignoring body effect: $(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})r_{o1}$.

Voltage gain: from (3) and (1):

$$-v_{out}G_{1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+v_{x}B$$
$$v_{x}=v_{out}\frac{G_{1}+C}{N}$$

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
-\frac{g_{m1}N}{G_{1}(N+B)+BC}$$

This can be written as

$$A_{v} = -G_{m}R_{out}$$

where the short-circuit transconductance is

$$G_{m}=g_{m1}\frac{N}{N+B}=g_{m1}
\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}
{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}\approx g_{m1}$$

since $g_{m2}\gg g_{ds1,2}$. Hence to very good
approximation:

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}R_{out}$$

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\,[R_{1}\parallel
\{(1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2})r_{o1}\}]$$

Ideal load:

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o1}[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]$$

$\approx -(g_{m1}r_{o1})(g_{m2}r_{o2})$.
This is the intrinsic gain squared.

In practice $R_{1}$ is finite, e.g. a PMOS
current source with $r_{op}$. Then

$$R_{out}\approx r_{op}\parallel g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}
\approx r_{op}$$

and $A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{op}$, only about
2x the simple CS with active load. The big
gain increase comes only if the load is also
cascoded.

Intuition:

$M_{1}$ produces $g_{m1}v_{in}$. Almost all
flows into $R_{out}$ to give $-g_{m1}R_{out}$.
$M_{2}$ shields the output from $X$, raising
the impedance seen at the drain by $\approx
g_{m2}r_{o2}$.

Node $X$: From (3),

$$\frac{v_{x}}{v_{in}}=A_{v}\frac{G_{1}+C}{N}$$

If $R_{1}$ is of order $r_{o}$, $|v_{x}/v_{in}|
\approx g_{m1}/g_{m2}\sim 1$. The Miller
multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is $1-A_{v1}\sim 2$,
not $1+g_{m1}R_{out}$. This pushes the input
pole out and is the main bandwidth advantage
of cascode.

If $R_{1}\to\infty$, $G_{1}\to 0$, then
$v_{x}/v_{in}\to -g_{m1}r_{o1}$, large, because
with an open drain the CG source impedance
becomes large: $R_{x}\approx (R_{1}+r_{o2})/
[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]\parallel r_{o1}$.
Low $R_{x}\approx 1/(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})$ requires
low $R_{1}$.

Frequency: $R_{in}=\infty$ at low frequency.
Dominant pole usually at output:

$$\omega_{p,out}\approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{out}}$$

$C_{out}=C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{I1}+C_{L}$.
Non-dominant pole at $X$:

$$\omega_{p,X}\approx \frac{1}{R_{x}C_{x}}$$

$C_{x}=C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1}$ (Miller),
$R_{x}$ as above, generally much higher than
$\omega_{p,out}$.

answer.text:
This is a single-ended telescopic cascode.

* $M_{1}$ : NMOS common-source input device
* $M_{2}$ : NMOS common-gate cascode device, gate DC bias $V_{b1}$
* $I_{1}$ : active load from $V_{DD}$ to output. In small signal
it is an AC ground through $R_{I1}$. Ideal $R_{I1}=\infty $.
Realistic PMOS: $R_{I1}=r_{op}$, for PMOS cascode: $\approx g_{mp}r_{op}^{2}$.

Assume all in saturation. $\lambda \ne 0$. Bulk of NMOS
is p-sub = GND, so $M_{1}$ has $V_{SB1}=0$, $M_{2}$
has $V_{SB2}=V_{X}>0$ and suffers body effect, $g_{mb2}\ne 0$.
If triple well with body to source, put $g_{mb2}=0$.

### Intuition

$M_{1}$ converts $v_{in}$ to current. $M_{2}$, with AC
grounded gate, conveys that current to the high impedance
output node with $\approx 1$ current gain, but presents a
low impedance to the drain of $M_{1}$.

Hence:

* gain is $g_{m1}\times$ impedance at output,
* impedance at output is boosted by cascode,
* Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is $\approx 1+g_{m1}R_{X}$
with $R_{X}$ small, bandwidth is much larger than simple
common source.

### DC operation

Let DC bias current be $I_{D}$.

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}=I_{D}$$

$V_{X}=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}$

For $M_{1}$ sat:

$$V_{X}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH1}=V_{ov1}$$

For $M_{2}$ sat:

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}$$
$$V_{out}-V_{X}\ge V_{b1}-V_{X}-V_{TH2}$$
$$V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{TH2}$$

$V_{TH2}>V_{TH0}$ due to body effect.

Combined, to keep both saturated:

$$V_{b1}\ge V_{ov1}+V_{GS2}=V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}+V_{TH2}$$
$$V_{out,min}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}=V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$$

This is the beauty of cascode: minimum output is sum
of overdrives.

Maximum output is set by $I_{1}$ staying in saturation.
For PMOS $I_{1}$:

$$V_{out,max}=V_{DD}-|V_{ovp}|$$

So usable swing:

$$V_{ov1}+V_{ov2} \le V_{out}\le V_{DD}-|V_{ovp}|$$

Note: the DC value of $V_{out}$ is ill defined.
It is a high-$Z$ node fed by two nominally equal DC
currents: the cascode and $I_{1}$. Any mismatch drives
$V_{out}$ to $V_{DD}$ or to triode. In practice the
stage cannot be open-loop biased; it needs feedback /
following stage to define $V_{out}$.

### Low frequency small signal

Gate $M_{2}$ AC ground. Source $M_{1}$ AC ground.
$v_{gs1}=v_{in}$.

Let $r_{o1}=1/g_{ds1}$, $r_{o2}=1/g_{ds2}$.

#### Impedance looking down from output

Turn off $v_{in}$, apply $v_{x}$ at $V_{out}$, measure $i_{x}$.

$M_{1}$ presents $r_{o1}$ from node $X$ to ground.

$M_{2}$ is a common-gate with source degeneration $R_{S}=r_{o1}$
and body effect.

KCL gives:

$$i_{x}=g_{m2}(-v_{S})+g_{mb2}(-v_{S})+g_{ds2}(v_{x}-v_{S})$$
$$i_{x}=v_{S}/r_{o1}$$

Hence:

$$R_{down}=\frac{v_{x}}{i_{x}}=r_{o2}+[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}]r_{o1}$$

$$R_{down}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}r_{o1}$$

$$\approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}r_{o1}$$

This is $\approx g_{m}r_{o}$ times larger than $r_{o1}$ alone.

Total output resistance:

$$R_{out}=R_{down}\parallel R_{I1}$$

If $I_{1}$ ideal, $R_{out}=R_{down}$. If $I_{1}$ is
simple PMOS, $R_{I1}=r_{op}\ll R_{down}$ and
$R_{out}\approx r_{op}$.

#### Voltage gain

With $v_{in}$ applied, let $v_{S}$ be small signal at $X$.

$$i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{S}$$
$$i_{d2}=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{S}+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_{S})$$

KCL $X$: $i_{d2}=i_{d1}$
KCL out, open: $i_{d2}+v_{out}/R_{I1}=0$

Solving, the Norton short circuit current into a shorted
output is:

$$I_{sc}=-g_{m1}v_{in}\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}\approx -g_{m1}v_{in}$$

Then $v_{out}=I_{sc}R_{out}$:

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-g_{m1}R_{out}\frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}{g_{ds1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}$$

$$\approx -g_{m1}R_{out}$$

Explicitly:

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}\left\{\left[r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}r_{o1}\right]\parallel R_{I1}\right\}$$

Special cases:

* Ideal load, no body: $A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o1}(g_{m2}r_{o2}+1)\approx -(g_{m1}r_{o1})(g_{m2}r_{o2})$
Intrinsic gain squared.
* Finite PMOS load $R_{I1}=r_{op}$: $A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}(r_{o1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\parallel r_{op})\approx -g_{m1}r_{op}$ if $r_{op}$ dominates. Cascode does not increase low frequency gain much but still helps bandwidth.
* PMOS cascode load $R_{I1}\approx (g_{mp}+g_{mbp})r_{op}^{2}$: both sides $\sim g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$, $R_{out}\approx \tfrac12 g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$, very high gain.

Input resistance:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

at low frequency.

#### Voltage at cascode node

$$ \frac{v_{X}}{v_{in}}\approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \approx -1 $$

Thus $V_{DS1}$ hardly moves - cascode shielding. Gain from gate to $X$ is small.

Impedance looking into source of $M_{2}$:

$$R_{X}=\frac{R_{I1}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}$$

for moderate $R_{I1}$. In parallel with $r_{o1}$.

### High frequency intuition

Low frequency dominant pole at output:

$$\omega_{p,out}\approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{out}}$$

$$C_{out}\approx C_{DB2}+C_{GD2}+C_{I1}+C_{L}$$

$R_{out}$ large, so dominant.

Non-dominant pole at $X$:

$$\omega_{pX}\approx \frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}{C_{X}}$$

$$C_{X}\approx C_{DB1}+C_{SB2}+C_{GS2}+C_{GD1}(1-A_{v1}^{-1})$$

Since $R_{X}$ is $\sim 1/g_{m}$, this pole is much higher than in a non-cascode stage. Miller effect of $C_{gd1}$ is only $(1+g_{m1}R_{X})\approx 2$, not $(1+g_{m1}R_{out})$.

Hence cascode achieves high gain and wide bandwidth simultaneously.

In summary: high-gain, high-output-impedance inverting amplifier with $A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}R_{out}$, $R_{in}=\infty$, $R_{out}$ boosted to $\sim g_{m}r_{o}^{2}$.

answer.text:
This is a single ended cascode with active load.

* $M_{1}$ : input common-source, source grounded.
* $M_{2}$ : common-gate cascode device, gate at AC ground $V_{b1}$.
* $I_{1}$ : DC load current from $V_{DD}$. AC impedance $R_{P}$.

$r_{o}=1/\lambda I_{D}$ . The current flows downward:
$I_{D2}=I_{D1}=I_{1}$ in DC steady state.

Bulk of an n-well NMOS is normally the p-sub = GND.
$M_{1}$: $V_{SB1}=0$, no back gate.
$M_{2}$: $V_{SB2}=V_{X}>0$,

$$v_{gs2}=-v_{x}\;, \quad v_{bs2}=-v_{x}$$

unless M2 is put in its own well tied to $X$. Keep
$g_{mb2}$ in formulas. Put $g_{mb2}=0$ if no body effect.

### 1. DC bias

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in,DC}>V_{TH1}$$
$$I_{D1}=\frac12 \mu_{n}C_{ox}\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_{1}V_{ov1}^{2}(1+\lambda_{n}V_{DS1})$$
$$V_{X}=V_{DS1}=V_{b1}-V_{GS2}$$

For saturation:

$$V_{X}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH1}=V_{ov1}$$
$$V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{X}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}=V_{ov2}$$

Hence

$$V_{out,min}=V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$$
$$V_{b1}\ge V_{ov1}+V_{GS2}=V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}+V_{TH2}$$

for minimum headroom. Above:

$$V_{out,max}=V_{DD}-V_{SDsat,I1}$$

to keep the PMOS current source in saturation.

Note the DC problem: the output node sees two high
impedances to $V_{DD}$ and to GND. $V_{out,DC}$ is floating.
Any $\Delta I = I_{1}-I_{D1}$ is multiplied by the large $R_{out}$
and drives $V_{out}$ to $V_{DD}$ or to triode.
In practice the bias needs feedback.

Large signal gain is very sharp. Linear input range is
$\sim V_{ov1}$.

### 2. Small signal low frequency

Model $M_{1}$: $g_{m1}v_{in}$ from $X$ to ground in parallel with $r_{o1}$.

Model $M_{2}$: gate grounded, source $X$, drain $V_{out}$:

drain to source current

$$i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+g_{mb2}v_{bs2}+g_{ds2}v_{ds2}$$
$$=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{x}}{r_{o2}}$$

$I_{1}$ : $R_{P}$ to AC ground.

KCL $X$:

$$i_{d2}=g_{m1}v_{in}+\frac{v_{x}}{r_{o1}} \tag{1}$$

KCL $V_{out}$, open:

$$i_{d2}+\frac{v_{out}}{R_{P}}=0 \tag{2}$$

Hence from (1)-(2)

$$ -\frac{v_{out}}{R_{P}}=g_{m1}v_{in}+\frac{v_{x}}{r_{o1}} $$

#### Output resistance

Set $v_{in}=0$, drive $v_{out}=v_{t}$, measure $i_{t}$.
$M_{1}$ is $r_{o1}$ from $X$ to ground.

From above with $v_{in}=0$:

$$\frac{v_{x}}{r_{o1}}=-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+\frac{v_{t}-v_{x}}{r_{o2}}$$

$$v_{t}=v_{x}\left[1+\frac{r_{o2}}{r_{o1}}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]$$

The current supplied by the test source into $M_{2}$ drain
is $v_{x}/r_{o1}$. So impedance looking into $M_{2}$ drain is:

$$R_{casc}=\frac{v_{t}}{v_{x}/r_{o1}}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

$$R_{out}=R_{casc}\parallel R_{P}$$

i.e. the standard CG with source degeneration $r_{o1}$:

$$R_{casc}\approx \left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]r_{o1}$$

This is $(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}$ times larger than a simple
common source $r_{o1}$. $M_{2}$ shields $M_{1}$ drain from $v_{out}$.

#### Voltage gain

From (2):

$$-(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})v_{x}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{x}}{r_{o2}}+\frac{v_{out}}{R_{P}}=0$$

$$v_{out}\left(\frac1{r_{o2}}+\frac1{R_{P}}\right)=v_{x}\left(g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)$$

Let $A=1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}$, $G=A/r_{o2}$.
Using $v_{x}=-r_{o1}(v_{out}/R_{P}+g_{m1}v_{in})$:

$$A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}= -\frac{g_{m1}r_{o1}R_{P}A}{R_{P}+r_{o2}+r_{o1}A}$$

with $r_{o2}+r_{o1}A=R_{casc}$. In other words

$$A_{v}=-g_{m1}R_{out}\,\frac{r_{o1}A}{r_{o2}+r_{o1}A}$$

$$\frac{r_{o1}A}{r_{o2}+r_{o1}A}=\frac{1}{1+\frac{r_{o2}}{r_{o1}A}}\approx 1$$

because $A\approx g_{m}r_{o}\gg 1$. Hence to very good
approximation

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}R_{out}$$

The cascode passes the $M_{1}$ signal current almost
entirely to the load. The effective $G_{m}\approx g_{m1}$.

Special cases:

* Ideal load $R_{P}\to\infty$:

$$R_{out}\approx r_{o1}A,\quad A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o1}A$$
$$=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\left[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\right]$$

Neglect body:

$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o1}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})\approx -(g_{m}r_{o})^{2}$$

if devices matched.

* Realistic single PMOS load $R_{P}=r_{o3}\sim r_{o1,2}$:

$$R_{casc}\gg r_{o3}\;\Rightarrow\; R_{out}\approx r_{o3}$$
$$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}r_{o3}$$

i.e. cascoding the input alone does not raise the gain
much if the load is not cascoded. To get $(g_{m}r_{o})^{2}$
gain you need cascode load as well – telescopic cascode.

Input resistance low frequency:

$$R_{in}=\infty$$

### 3. What the cascode buys

Voltage at intermediate node $X$:

$$A_{x}=\frac{v_{x}}{v_{in}}=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\frac{R_{P}+r_{o2}}{R_{P}+r_{o2}+r_{o1}A}$$

If $R_{P}\sim r_{o}$:

$$A_{x}\approx -g_{m1}\frac{R_{P}+r_{o2}}{A}\approx -1\;{\rm to}\;-{\rm few}$$

versus $-g_{m1}R_{out}$ for a simple CS. Hence:

* Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is $1-A_{x}$, small.
  Input capacitance $\approx C_{gs1}+(1-A_{x})C_{gd1}$
  is much reduced. Input pole pushed out.
* Reverse isolation improved, stage almost unilateral.
* Output impedance greatly increased.
* Drain of $M_{1}$ sees only small swing, suppressing
  $\lambda$-effect on $M_{1}$ and improving current-mirror accuracy.

Cost is headroom $V_{ov2}$, an extra non-dominant pole at $X$,
and bias complexity.

Frequency estimate: dominant pole at output

$$\omega_{p,out}\approx \frac{1}{R_{out}C_{out}}$$
$$C_{out}\approx C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{db,I1}+C_{gd,I1}+C_{L}$$

Pole at $X$:

$$C_{X}\approx C_{db1}+C_{gd1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gb2}$$
$$R_{X}\approx \left[\frac{R_{P}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}\right]\parallel r_{o1}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}$$

$$\omega_{pX}\approx \frac{1}{R_{X}C_{X}}\approx \frac{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}{C_{X}}$$

Much higher than $\omega_{p,out}$ because $R_{X}$ is low.
That is why the cascode has wider bandwidth than a CS
with the same gain.

The stage is a telescopic NMOS cascode.

* $M_{1}$ is a common-source device.
* $M_{2}$ is a common-gate device, $V_{b1}$ being a dc bias and therefore
an ac ground.
* $I_{1}$ is the active load. Let its small-signal resistance be $R_{1}$;
for an ideal current source $R_{1}\to\infty$.
* The signal current is developed at node $X$ and taken out at the
drain of $M_{2}$.

Assume midband operation, i.e. neglect device capacitances, and
$M_{1},M_{2}$ in saturation. Put
$g_m'=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$ for $M_{2}$, whose source is above ground.
If the body of $M_{2}$ is tied to its source, $g_{mb2}=0$.

### 1.  DC bias

The same current flows in $M_{1},M_{2}$ and $I_{1}$:

$$
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}
      =\frac12\mu_nC_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_1V_{ov1}^{2}
      =\frac12\mu_nC_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_2V_{ov2}^{2}
$$
ignoring $\lambda$ for the bias calculation, with
$V_{ov i}=V_{GSi}-V_{THi}$, 
$$
g_{mi}=\frac{2I_{1}}{V_{ovi}},\qquad 
r_{oi}=\frac1{\lambda_i I_{1}} .
$$

The intermediate voltage is
$$
V_X = V_{b1}-V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}-V_{ov2},
\qquad V_{DS1}=V_X,\;\; V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_X .
$$
$V_{TH2}$ is increased by body effect if the substrate is grounded,
$V_{BS2}=-V_X$.
In saturation
$$
V_X\ge V_{ov1},\qquad V_{out}-V_X\ge V_{ov2}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{TH2}.
$$
The lowest useful $V_{b1}$, $V_{b1}\approx V_{ov1}+V_{TH2}+V_{ov2}$,
gives
$$
V_{out,\min}\approx V_{ov1}+V_{ov2},
$$
the usual headroom penalty of a cascode. At the top,
$V_{out,\max}\approx V_{DD}-V_{I1,\min}$, where $V_{I1,\min}$ is the
voltage $I_{1}$ needs to stay in saturation. The quiescent $V_{out}$ is
set by the realisation of $I_{1}$; an ideal $I_{1}$ in series with an
ideal gate-controlled stack leaves it indeterminate.

### 2.  Small-signal gain and resistances

Input resistance, at the gate of $M_{1}$,
$$
R_{in}\approx\infty\qquad\text{(low frequency).}
$$

Resistance looking into the drain of the cascode, with $v_{in}=0$,
is obtained by a test source at the output. The resistance seen
at $X$ is $r_{o1}$, and $M_{2}$ boosts it by its intrinsic gain:

$$
\,R_{down}=r_{o2}+\bigl[\,1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\bigr]r_{o1}\,
      \approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,r_{o1}r_{o2}\quad (g_mr_o\gg1)
$$

Hence
$$
\,R_{out}=R_{down}\parallel R_{1}\,\qquad 
\bigl(R_{1}\!\to\!\infty:\;R_{out}\approx(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}\bigr)
$$
i.e. about $(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}$ times larger than $r_{o1}$ alone.
An external load $R_L$ is included by $R_1\to R_1\parallel R_L$.

The (exact, to first order) midband voltage gain is

$$
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
 =-\,g_{m1}\,
   \frac{\bigl[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\bigr]r_{o1}R_{1}}
        {R_{1}+R_{down}}
\;\approx\;
-\,g_{m1}\bigl(R_{down}\parallel R_{1}\bigr).
$$

For an ideal load,
$$
\,A_v\approx -g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,r_{o1}r_{o2}\,
$$
negative, i.e. inverting, of order $(g_mr_o)^2$ for matched devices.
The short-circuit transconductance remains $\approx g_{m1}$; the
cascode does not increase $G_m$, it increases the resistance into
which $G_m$ works.

The voltage at the internal node is
$$
\frac{v_x}{v_{in}}\approx -g_{m1}\Bigl(r_{o1}\parallel 
\frac{R_{1}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}\Bigr),
\qquad 
\frac{v_{out}}{v_x}= \bigl[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\bigr]
\frac{R_{1}}{R_{1}+r_{o2}}>0 ,
$$
so $|v_x/v_{in}|\ll |A_v|$: the Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$
is set by the gain to $X$, not by the full gain.

### 3.  Remarks

* Dominant pole is normally at the output,
$\omega_{p,out}\approx1/(R_{out}C_L)$. The pole at $X$,
$\omega_{pX}\approx1/(R_XC_X)$ with $C_X$ the small capacitance at
$X$ ($C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+\cdots$), is much higher; the stage is
considerably faster, for a given gain, than a simple common-source
stage, and has good reverse isolation.
* Costs: an extra $V_{ov}$ of headroom and reduced output swing,
an extra bias $V_{b1}$, and the noise and finite $R_{1}$ of the
real current source $I_{1}$, which in practice limit the
$(g_mr_o)^2$ gain above. Large-signal rise of a capacitive load
is slew-limited by $I_{1}/C_L$.

In short: $M_{1}$ converts $v_{in}$ to a current $\approx g_{m1}v_{in}$,
$M_{2}$ passes that current to a load while raising the output
resistance from $r_o$ to $\sim g_mr_o^{2}$, giving a high-gain,
wideband, inverting telescopic cascode stage.

answer.text:
The circuit is a **telescopic cascode common-source stage**. $M_1$ is the input common-source device, $M_2$ is a common-gate cascode device, $V_{b1}$ is a fixed bias (a.c. ground) and $I_1$ is an active load.

### 1. d.c. bias

Both devices carry the same current,

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1 .
\]

With $\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$ and ignoring $\lambda$,

\[
I_1=\tfrac12\beta_1V_{OV1}^{2}=\tfrac12\beta_2V_{OV2}^{2},
\qquad 
g_{mi}=\frac{2I_1}{V_{OVi}}, \qquad 
r_{oi}=\frac{1}{\lambda_iI_1}.
\]

The required input bias is

\[
V_{in,DC}=V_{TH1}+V_{OV1},
\]

and the voltage at the internal node $\,X$ is

\[
V_X = V_{b1}-V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}-V_{OV2}=V_{DS1}.
\]

Note that $M_2$ suffers body effect if its bulk is the (grounded) substrate, since $V_{BS2}=-V_X$. Then $V_{TH2}$ is raised and the effective transconductance of $M_2$ is $g_{m2}'=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$. (If the bulk is tied to its source, use just $g_{m2}$.)

For both devices to stay in saturation:

* $M_1$: $\;V_X\ge V_{OV1}$, i.e. $\;V_{b1}\ge V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}+V_{TH2}$,
* $M_2$: $\;V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{TH2}$.

Hence the lowest permissible output voltage is $V_{b1}-V_{TH2}$, and the highest is set by the compliance of $I_1$, $V_{DD}-V_{I_1,\min}$. This extra stacked $V_{GS}$ is the headroom price paid for cascoding. The optimum (lowest) $V_{b1}$ is the value which just keeps $M_1$ saturated.

### 2. Small-signal gain and output resistance

With $V_{b1}$ at a.c. ground, $M_2$ presents a source-degenerated output looking into its drain. The resistance looking into the drain of the cascode is

\[
R_{out,N}=r_{o2}+\bigl[1+g_{m2}'r_{o2}\bigr]r_{o1}
\;\approx\;g_{m2}'\,r_{o1}r_{o2},
\qquad g_{m2}'=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}.
\]

$M_1$'s output resistance $r_{o1}$ is boosted by roughly $g_{m2}'r_{o2}$ — this is the main job of $M_2$. The short-circuit transconductance is essentially unchanged, $G_m\approx g_{m1}$, because the cascode is a near-unity-gain current buffer. Therefore

\[
\boxed{\,A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}\approx -g_{m1}\Bigl(R_{out,N}\,\big\|\,R_{I_1}\Bigr)\,}
\]

where $R_{I_1}$ is the finite output resistance of the current source $I_1$. For an ideal $I_1$ ($R_{I_1}\!\to\!\infty$) this reduces to $A_v\approx-g_{m1}g_{m2}'r_{o1}r_{o2}$: compared with a simple common-source stage ($-g_{m1}r_{o1}$), the gain is multiplied by $\approx g_{m2}'r_{o2}$, the intrinsic gain of $M_2$. In practice a real (e.g. PMOS) current source will limit $R_{out}$ to $R_{out,N}\|R_{I_1}$.

Other terminal properties:

* **Input resistance:** $R_{in}\approx\infty$ (gate of $M_1$); at high frequency it is capacitive.
* **Resistance at node $X$:** looking into the source of $M_2$,
  \[
  R_X=r_{o1}\;\Big\|\;\frac{R_{I_1}+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}'r_{o2}}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{g_{m2}'}
  \]
  for a practical (finite) load. $X$ is therefore a low-impedance node.

### 3. Why the cascode is used

* **High gain / high $R_{out}$**, as above, without a larger load resistor.
* **Suppressed Miller effect.** The gain from the input to $M_1$'s drain (node $X$) is only
  \[
  \frac{v_x}{v_{in}}\approx-\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}'}\approx -1,
  \]
  instead of the full $|A_v|$. Hence $C_{gd1}$ is multiplied by $\approx(1+g_{m1}/g_{m2}')\approx2$, not by $(1+|A_v|)$, so $C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gd1}(1+g_{m1}/g_{m2}')$ is small and the input pole stays high.
* **High-frequency pole at $X$:** $\omega_{pX}\approx g_{m2}'/C_X$ with $C_X\approx C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1}$. Since $R_X$ is small this pole is far out; the dominant pole is normally at the output, $\omega_{p,out}\approx1/(R_{out}C_L)$.
* **Noise:** the input-referred noise is dominated by $M_1$ (and by $I_1$, referred back through $g_{m1}$). $M_2$'s noise is source-degenerated by $r_{o1}$ and contributes negligibly.

### 4. Summary

| Property | Result |
|---|---|
| Topology | NMOS telescopic cascode CS stage, active load $I_1$ |
| Bias current | $I_1$ in both $M_1$, $M_2$ |
| Voltage gain | $-g_{m1}\bigl(g_{m2}'r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\|\;R_{I_1}\bigr)$ |
| Output resistance | $\approx g_{m2}'r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\|\;R_{I_1}$ |
| Input resistance | $\approx\infty$ (capacitive) |
| Min. output voltage | $V_{b1}-V_{TH2}$ |
| Main cost | Reduced swing/headroom, extra bias $V_{b1}$ |

In short: $M_1$ converts $v_{in}$ to a current, $M_2$ passes that current to the output while shielding $M_1$ from $v_{out}$ and boosting the output resistance by $\sim g_{m2}'r_{o2}$. The result is a much higher-gain, wider-bandwidth inverting amplifier than a single common-source device, at the expense of output swing.

answer.text:
The circuit is an NMOS cascode common-source stage.
$M_{1}$ is the input transconductor, $M_{2}$ is a common-gate
cascode device, $V_{b1}$ is its gate bias and $I_{1}$ is an
active load.  The body of $M_{1}$ is tied to its source, and
the body of $M_{2}$ is tied to its source at $X$, so as drawn

$$V_{BS1}=V_{BS2}=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g_{mb1}=g_{mb2}=0$$

i.e. there is no body effect in $M_{2}$.

### 1.  DC operation

$M_{1}$, $M_{2}$ and $I_{1}$ are in series, hence, neglecting
gate current,

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}\equiv I_{D}$$

$$ 
V_{GS1}=V_{TH1}+V_{ov1},\qquad 
V_{GS2}=V_{TH2}+V_{ov2}
$$
$$V_{ov i}= \sqrt{\frac{2I_{D}}{\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i}}\;,\qquad 
g_{mi}=\frac{2I_D}{V_{ovi}},\qquad r_{oi}=\frac1{\lambda_i I_D} $$
with $V_{TH2}=V_{TH0}$, since $V_{BS2}=0$.

Node $X$ is fixed by $M_{2}$ acting as a source follower for
dc:
$$
V_X = V_{b1}-V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}-V_{ov2}=V_{DS1}.
$$
$M_{1}$ in saturation requires $V_{DS1}\ge V_{ov1}$, i.e.

$$
V_{b1}\ge V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}+V_{TH2}.
$$

$M_{2}$ in saturation requires $V_{DS2}\ge V_{ov2}$, i.e.

$$
V_{out}\ge V_X+V_{ov2}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}.
$$

In addition $V_{out}$ must leave compliance for the real
device implementing $I_{1}$, $V_{out}\le V_{DD}-V_{I1}$.
Choosing $V_{b1}$ at its minimum value maximises swing:
the lowest permissible output is approximately
$V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$, which is the headroom penalty of the
cascode over a simple common-source stage.

### 2.  Small-signal gain and resistances

Let $R_{L}$ be the (finite) small-signal resistance of the
realisation of $I_{1}$, in parallel with any external load.
The small-signal drain current of $M_{2}$ is
$i_{d2}=-g_{m2}v_x+(v_{out}-v_x)/r_{o2}$, since its gate is at
ac ground and $v_{bs2}=0$, and $i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+v_x/r_{o1}$,
with $i_{d1}=i_{d2}$.

The resistance looking into the drain of the cascode,
$v_{in}=0$, is the common-gate resistance boosted by
source degeneration $r_{o1}$:

$$
\,R_{\rm down}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}
      \approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\,\qquad g_mr_o\gg1
$$

i.e. about $g_{m2}r_{o2}$ times the $r_{o1}$ of a simple CS
stage.  Hence

$$
R_{out}=R_{\rm down}\,\|\,R_{L}.
$$

The short-circuit transconductance is essentially $g_{m1}$,
so, to the usual $1/g_mr_o$ accuracy,

$$
\,A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}\approx -\,g_{m1}\bigl(R_{\rm down}\|R_L\bigr)\,
$$

$$
R_{in}\approx\infty\quad\text{(gate input).}
$$

For the idealised load drawn, $R_L\to\infty$, 
$$
A_v=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\bigl(1+g_{m2}r_{o2}\bigr)\approx
-\,(g_{m1}r_{o1})(g_{m2}r_{o2}), 
\qquad R_{out}\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2},
$$
of the order of the square of the intrinsic gain $g_mr_o$.
Physically $M_{1}$ gives gain to $X$ and the CG device
gives further gain to the output.

In practice $R_L$ is, e.g., the $r_o$ of a PMOS current
source.  Then $R_{out}\approx R_L$ and $A_v\approx -g_{m1}R_L$:
the full benefit is obtained only if the load is also
cascoded, as in a telescopic-cascode op-amp.

The impedance at the intermediate node is low for a
realistic $R_L$,
$$
R_X = r_{o1}\left\|\frac{R_L+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}}
      \approx r_{o1}\right\|\frac1{g_{m2}},
$$
so $v_x/v_{in}=-g_{m1}R_X$ is small, of order $-g_{m1}/g_{m2}$.
This is the well known shielding action of the cascode:
$V_X$ is almost fixed, the Miller multiplication of
$C_{gd1}$ is greatly reduced, reverse isolation is good,
and bandwidth is much better than a simple CS stage with
the same gain.

### 3.  Frequency response, swing and practical remarks

Dominant pole, at the high-impedance output node:
$$
\omega_{p,out}\approx
\frac{1}{R_{out}\,(C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{I1}+C_L)} ,
\qquad\text{GBW}\approx \frac{g_{m1}}{C_L}\; .
$$
Non-dominant pole at $X$:
$$
\omega_{pX}\approx
\frac{1}{R_X\,(C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1})},
$$
normally at high frequency because $R_X\sim1/g_{m2}$.
The input pole is set by the source resistance and
$C_{gs1}+C_{gd1}(1-v_x/v_{in})$.

Input-referred noise is dominated by $M_{1}$ and by the
load $I_{1}$; the noise of the cascode device $M_{2}$ is
degenerated by $r_{o1}$ and is largely suppressed at low
frequencies.  $V_{b1}$ must be a clean ac ground, as noise
on it is transmitted to the output through $g_{m2}$.

Remarks:

* High gain and high $R_{out}$, good isolation and
bandwidth, at the cost of at least $V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$
(plus load) of output headroom and a bias $V_{b1}$.
Open-loop dc $V_{out}$ is ill-defined with two high
impedance devices in series: $I_{1}$ must accurately match
the current set by $V_{in}$, otherwise the stage saturates.
* Tying the body of $M_{2}$ to $X$ removes the body effect,
keeps $V_{TH2}$ low and saves headroom, at the price of
$R_{\rm down}\propto g_{m2}$ rather than $g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$.
In a standard $p$-substrate CMOS process NMOS bodies are
the common substrate and cannot be tied separately to $X$;
this connection requires discrete devices, triple-well or
SOI. With body to ground, replace $g_{m2}$ by $g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$
in $R_{\rm down}$ and use the body-effected $V_{TH2}(V_X)$.

The two-transistor stack M1–M2 that is connected to the ideal current-sink I1 is nothing more than a single–ended cascode amplifier:

1. What each device is doing  
   • M1 : signal device (common-source).  
   • M2 : cascode device whose gate is fixed at the bias voltage Vb1; it keeps the drain of M1 (node X) at an almost constant voltage, greatly increasing the small-signal output resistance.  
   • I1 : an (almost) infinite-resistance load that forces a dc current I1 through the MOS pair.  
   • Vout : the high-impedance output node.  

2. DC (large–signal) analysis  
   Assume both transistors are to be biased in saturation.

   a) Drain current  
      I D1 = I D2 = I1                                             (1)

   b) Voltage at the internal node X  
      VX ≃ VGS1 = Vov1 + VTH1                                      (2)  

      where Vov1 = VGS1 – VTH1 is the over-drive of M1.

   c) Bias for the cascode gate  
      The gate of M2 must be high enough to let I1 flow but low enough to leave M2 in saturation over the full output-voltage range:

      VB1 ≃ VX + Vov2 + VTH2                                       (3)

   d) Output-voltage compliance  
      • For M2 to stay in saturation: VDS2 ≥ Vov2  
        ⇒ Vout,min ≃ VX + Vov2 = Vov1 + VTH1 + Vov2                (4)

      • For the current source to stay in saturation:  
        VDS,I1 ≥ VDSsat,I1 ⇒ Vout,max ≃ VDD – VDSsat,I1            (5)

      Hence the admissible output swing is

           ΔVout ≃ VDD – VDSsat,I1 – (Vov1 + VTH1 + Vov2).         (6)

3. Small-signal (incremental) model  
   With ro,I1 ≫ ro2, ro1 we can neglect the finite output resistance of I1.

   Small-signal parameters  
      gm1 , ro1 → M1  
      gm2 , ro2 → M2  

   Node equations  

      At node X :   –gm1·vin – (vx/ro1) – gm2·vx   + (vout – vx)/ro2 = 0
      At node Vout: +(vx – vout)/ro2 – (vout/roI1)                   ≈ 0

      (roI1 → ∞ ⇒ the second term vanishes.)

   Solving for the open-circuit gain Av = vout / vin gives, to first order,

           Av ≃ –gm1 · (gm2·ro2·ro1 + ro2 + ro1)                   (7)

      Because the cascode raises the resistance seen looking into M2’s drain,

           rout ≃ ro2 + gm2·ro2·ro1  ≈ gm2·ro2·ro1                  (8)

      and since ro1,ro2 ≫ 1/gm1 , Av reduces to

           Av ≃ – gm1 · rout ≃ – gm1 gm2 ro1 ro2.                  (9)

      If ro1 ≃ ro2 ≃ ro,

           Av ≃ – gm1 gm2 ro².                                     (10)

      Thus the gain is the product of the two g m ’s multiplied by the square of a single-device r o – often hundreds or thousands, i.e. tens of decibels.

4. Salient features of the topology  
   • Very high intrinsic gain because rout is boosted by the cascode.  
   • Node X is nearly ac-ground (small swing ≈ vx ≪ vout), so the Miller capacitance of M1 is suppressed and the input pole is shifted to a higher frequency.  
   • Good power-supply rejection: the high-resistance current source isolates Vout from VDD noise.  
   • Output swing is limited on the low side by two over-drives plus one threshold, on the high side by the current-source compliance.  
   • Only one bias voltage (Vb1) is required for the cascode.

5. Practical design procedure  
   1) Choose I1 from the required transconductance gm1 (gm1 ≈ 2·I1 / Vov1).  
   2) Pick Vov1 (speed vs. swing trade-off), giving VX from (2).  
   3) Choose Vov2 (typically 150–200 mV) and determine Vb1 from (3).  
   4) Check that the resulting Vout,min from (4) leaves enough room for the desired signal swing below VDD – VDSsat,I1.  
   5) Lay out M2 with a longer channel (larger ro2) if still higher gain is needed.

In short, the circuit is a classical n-channel cascode stage: a common-source transistor M1 loaded by a current sink, with its drain shielded by a common-gate device M2 that dramatically increases the output resistance and hence the voltage gain, at the expense of reduced output-voltage swing.

gm2(VB1 – vX) + (vX – vOUT)/ro2  =  gm1 vIN + vX/ro1

vX ≈ [gm1 / (gm2 + 1/ro2)]  vIN  ≈  (gm1 / gm2) vIN    for  gm2ro2 ≫ 1.  (5)

Rout ≡ vT / iT  ≈  ro2 + (1 + gm2ro2)ro1                 (6)

Rout ≈ roI + (gm2ro2 ro1) + (ro1 ∥ ro2).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
Av  =  vOUT / vIN  =  –gm1 · Rout                        (7)

M1   converts vIN to a drain current (g m1).

### 4. Key Characteristics & Analysis

**A. High Output Impedance**
The primary advantage of the cascode structure is a significant increase in output impedance.
*   Looking down into the drain of $M_2$ (from node $V_{out}$), the output resistance is boosted by the intrinsic gain of $M_2$.
*   $R_{out, cascode} \approx g_{m2} r_{o2} r_{o1}$ (where $g_m$ is transconductance and $r_o$ is output resistance).
*   The total output resistance at $V_{out}$ is the parallel combination of the cascode resistance and the output resistance of the current source $I_1$ (let's call it $R_{I1}$).
    $$R_{total} = R_{I1} \parallel (g_{m2} r_{o2} r_{o1})$$

*   The transconductance of the entire cascode stage is approximately equal to that of the input transistor, $G_m \approx g_{m1}$.
*   The voltage gain $A_v$ is given by:
    $$A_v = -G_m \times R_{total} \approx -g_{m1} [R_{I1} \parallel (g_{m2} r_{o2} r_{o1})]$$
*   If the current source $I_1$ is ideal (infinite resistance), the gain becomes extremely high: $A_v \approx -g_{m1} g_{m2} r_{o1} r_{o2}$.

**C. Reduced Miller Effect (High Bandwidth)**
In a standard common-source amplifier, the gate-drain capacitance ($C_{gd}$) of the transistor is multiplied by the gain (Miller effect), creating a large effective input capacitance that limits bandwidth.
*   In this cascode circuit, the drain of $M_1$ (node $X$) is held at a relatively constant AC potential by the common-gate transistor $M_2$.
*   This minimizes the voltage swing at the drain of $M_1$, effectively eliminating the Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$. This allows the amplifier to operate at much higher frequencies.

### Summary
This circuit is a **high-gain, high-output-impedance amplifier**. It is designed to take a small input voltage signal at $V_{in}$ and produce a large amplified voltage signal at $V_{out}$, with improved frequency response compared to a single-transistor amplifier.

## 1. What the circuit is

It is an **NMOS cascode voltage amplifier** with an *active* (current‑source) load.

* **M₁** – common‑source stage (source grounded, gate = signal terminal $V_{in}$).
* **M₂** – common‑gate stage (gate held at the d.c. bias $V_{b1}$ = a.c. ground, drain = $V_{out}$).
* **$I_1$** – a current source from $V_{DD}$ that biases the stack and acts as the load (very high small‑signal resistance).
* Node **X** = drain of M₁ / source of M₂.

The port marks are the usual convention: filled dot = d.c. port ($V_{b1}$), open circles = small‑signal ports ($V_{in},\,V_{out}$). So for the a.c. analysis $v_{b1}=0$ and $v_{in}$ is the signal.

---

## 2. D.C. operating point

Because the gates draw no d.c. current and $V_{out}$ is open, the same current flows through both transistors:

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1$$

M₁ in saturation fixes $V_X$ (with $V_{GS1}=V_{in}^{DC}$):
$$I_1=\tfrac12 k_n\!_1\,(V_{in}^{DC}-V_{th1})^2(1+\lambda_1 V_X)$$

M₂ must be biased into saturation, i.e.
$$V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_X\ge V_{th2},\qquad V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_X\ge V_{OV2}$$
and it carries the same current:
$$I_1=\tfrac12 k_n\!_2\,(V_{b1}-V_X-V_{th2})^2(1+\lambda_2(V_{out}-V_X))$$

Thus $V_X$ is set by M₁, $V_{b1}$ is chosen as $V_{b1}\approx V_X+V_{OV2}$ to put M₂ in saturation, and $V_{out}$ settles at $V_X+V_{DS2}$, which must stay below $V_{DD}-V_{CS,min}$ so that the load current source $I_1$ remains in saturation. The only design freedom left is the ratio $k_n\!_1/k_n\!_2$ (or $V_{b1}$) to place $V_X$ where it is needed.

---

## 3. Small‑signal model

Let $v_x$ be the signal at node X and $v_o$ the signal at $V_{out}$.
M₁: $v_{gs1}=v_{in}$, $v_{s1}=0$.
M₂: $v_{gs2}=0-v_x=-v_x$ (gate at a.c. ground).

Using the standard hybrid‑$\pi$ model ($g_{m1},r_{o1}$ and $g_{m2},r_{o2}$):

* Current into M₁ drain (from X): $g_{m1}v_{in}+v_x/r_{o1}$
* Current into M₂ source (from X): $g_{m2}v_x-(v_o-v_x)/r_{o2}$

KCL at node X (no other branch):
$$g_{m1}v_{in}+\frac{v_x}{r_{o1}}+g_{m2}v_x-\frac{v_o-v_x}{r_{o2}}=0 \tag{1}$$

---

## 4. Results

**Open‑circuit voltage gain.** With $V_{out}$ open, $i_{d2}=0\Rightarrow (v_o-v_x)/r_{o2}=g_{m2}v_x$. Substituting in (1) gives $v_x=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\,v_{in}$ and $v_o=(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})v_x$, hence

$$\boxed{A_{oc}=\frac{v_o}{v_{in}}=-\,g_{m1}r_{o1}\,(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})\;\approx\;-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}}$$

(Equivalently $A_{oc}\approx -g_{m1}\,R_{out}$.) Note that the gain is split: M₁ gives $-g_{m1}r_{o1}$ to node X, and the common‑gate M₂ multiplies by $1+g_{m2}r_{o2}$.

**Input resistance:** $R_{in}=\infty$ (MOS gate of M₁).

**Output resistance** (the Thevenin resistance seen at $V_{out}$, with $v_{in}=0$ and a test source applied):

$$\boxed{R_{out}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}\,r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\approx\;g_{m2}\,r_{o1}r_{o2}}$$

This is the classic cascode result – roughly $g_{m2}r_{o1}$ times larger than a single stage.

**Loaded gain.** With a load $R_L$ at $V_{out}$:

$$A_v=A_{oc}\,\frac{R_L}{R_L+R_{out}}$$

**With body effect.** If M₂'s bulk is tied to ground (not to its source), $V_{SB2}=V_X>0$ raises $V_{th2}$ and adds $g_{mb2}v_{sb2}$ to the M₂ small‑signal equations; this slightly lowers $g_{m2}$ and reduces $R_{out}$ and the gain. If the bulk is tied to the source, $g_{mb2}=0$ and the formulas above hold exactly.

---

## 5. Why a cascode (frequency / bandwidth view)

* The high $R_{out}$ gives a large mid‑band gain and a high‑frequency pole $f_p\simeq 1/[2\pi R_{out}(C_{out}+C_L)]$.
* Node X is a **low‑impedance** node when the output is loaded: $Z_X\approx 1/g_{m2}$ (since the a.c. gain $v_x/v_{in}\approx -g_{m1}/g_{m2}\ll 1$). Therefore the Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is only $1+g_{m1}/g_{m2}\approx 1$, instead of $1+g_{m1}R_L$ in a plain common‑source stage. The input capacitance drops to $\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gd1}$, which is the main bandwidth advantage of the cascode.

---

### Summary
The figure is a **two‑stage NMOS cascode (CS + CG) amplifier** loaded by a current source $I_1$. It is biased so that $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1$ and both devices are in saturation ($V_{b1}$ sets the source‑gate bias of M₂). Small‑signal characteristics:

| Quantity | Expression | Approx. |
|---|---|---|
| $R_{in}$ | $\infty$ | – |
| $R_{out}$ | $r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$ | $g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$ |
| $A_{oc}$ | $-g_{m1}r_{o1}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})$ | $-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$ |
| $A_v(R_L)$ | $A_{oc}\,R_L/(R_L+R_{out})$ | – |

Its purpose is to deliver a **large inverting voltage gain with a very high output resistance**, and, by keeping node X at a low a.c. impedance, to **suppress the Miller effect** and thereby improve bandwidth relative to a single common‑source stage.

## 1. What the circuit is

It is an **NMOS cascode amplifier** with an **active (current‑source) load**.

* **M₁** – common‑source (CS) device: source to ground, gate = $V_{in}$, drain = node $X$. It provides the transconductance $g_{m1}$.
* **M₂** – common‑gate (CG) "cascode" device: source = node $X$, gate = fixed bias $V_{b1}$ (AC ground), drain = $V_{out}$. It provides a large output impedance and shields $C_{gs2}$ from $V_{out}$.
* **$I_1$** – the bias/load current source from $V_{DD}$ to $V_{out}$. It sets the DC operating current and (if its own $r_o$ is finite) appears in parallel with the stack at the output.

The current flows $V_{DD}\to I_1\to M_2\to M_1\to$ GND, consistent with two NMOS in series (arrows on the source terminals point outward).

## 2. DC operating point

Because $I_1$ is the only path, the bias current is forced:

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1$$

The bias voltages must be chosen so that **both** transistors stay in saturation:

* M₁ (CS): $V_X = V_{DS1}\ge V_{OV1}$, with $V_{in}\ge V_{th1}$ and $V_{in}$ set so that $I_{D1}=I_1$.
* M₂ (CG): $V_{b1}-V_X\ge V_{OV2}$ and $V_{out}-V_X\ge V_{OV2}$.

Hence the usual design rule is $V_X \approx V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}$ (or higher) and $V_{b1}=V_X+V_{OV2}$, i.e. $V_{b1}\ge V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}$. This is what gives the cascode its wide output swing:

$$V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}\;\lesssim\;V_{out}\;\lesssim\;V_{DD}-V_{headroom}(I_1)$$

## 3. Small‑signal model

Open $I_1$ (ideal source), $V_{b1}$ = AC ground. With $v_{gs1}=v_{in}$, $v_{gs2}=-v_x$, and including each $r_o$:

* **Node $X$:** $\;g_{m1}v_{in}+\dfrac{v_x}{r_{o1}}+g_{m2}v_x-\dfrac{v_{out}-v_x}{r_{o2}}=0$
* **Node $V_{out}$** (open, $R_L\to\infty$): $\;-g_{m2}v_x+\dfrac{v_{out}-v_x}{r_{o2}}=0\;\Rightarrow\;v_{out}=v_x(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})$

Solving the two equations:

$$v_x=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\,v_{in}$$

(The M₂ source draws no small‑signal current when its drain is open, so M₁'s drain current flows only through $r_{o1}$.)

## 4. Voltage gain

$$\boxed{A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-\,g_{m1}\,r_{o1}\,(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})\;\approx\;-g_{m1}g_{m2}\,r_{o1}r_{o2}}$$

Negative sign → inverting (from the CS stage). For large $g_mr_o$ the gain is the product of the two transconductances and the two output resistances — much larger than a single CS stage. If the load current source has finite $r_{o,I_1}$, it is simply placed in parallel at the output, reducing the magnitude.

## 5. Output resistance

Apply a test current at $V_{out}$ with $v_{in}=0$:

$$\boxed{R_{out}=r_{o1}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})+r_{o2}\;\approx\;g_{m2}\,r_{o1}r_{o2}}$$

(with an ideal load; with a real load $I_1$ use $R_{out}=r_{o,I_1}\parallel[\,r_{o1}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})+r_{o2}\,]$). This is the classic cascode result: $r_{o1}$ is "boosted" by $(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})$.

## 6. Input resistance

The signal enters the gate of M₁, so $R_{in}\to\infty$ (MOS gate). The node $X$ sees the CG input resistance $R_{in,CG}=(r_{o2}+R_L)/(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})$ in parallel with $r_{o1}$, which sets the first internal node, but it does not load the external $V_{in}$ terminal.

## 7. High‑frequency / bandwidth

Because the gate of M₂ is at AC ground, $C_{gs2}$ appears as a plain $C_{gs2}$ from $X$ to ground — **not** multiplied by the large gain. The cascode therefore removes the Miller multiplication that a second CS stage would impose on $V_{out}$, pushing the dominant pole up and improving the gain–bandwidth product relative to a two‑stage CS chain.

## 8. Summary of key results

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| Bias current | $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1$ |
| Bias constraint | $V_{b1}\ge V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}$ |
| Gain | $-g_{m1}r_{o1}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})\approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$ |
| Output resistance | $r_{o1}(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})+r_{o2}\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}$ |
| Input resistance | $\infty$ |
| $V_{out}$ swing | $V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}\;\lesssim\;V_{out}\;\lesssim\;V_{DD}-V_{I_1,headroom}$ |

In short: M₁ (CS) converts $V_{in}$ to a current, M₂ (CG) converts that current at a low‑gain internal node into a large output voltage across the high‑impedance stack, and $I_1$ biases the chain while acting as the load — yielding a high‑gain, high‑output‑impedance, wide‑swing, and bandwidth‑enhanced amplifier.

| Transistor | Drain | Gate | Source | Role |
|------------|-------|------|--------|------|
| M₁ | node X | $V_{in}$ | 0 V | common‑source (input) device |
| M₂ | $V_{out}$ | $V_{b1}$ | node X | common‑gate (cascode) device, gate at **AC ground** |

* $V_{b1}$ is a fixed DC bias (the “b” = bias), so the gate of M₂ is an AC short.
* The current source $I_1$ (arrow into the node) is the load; it fixes the DC bias current and, in small signal, appears as a finite output resistance $r_{oI}$ (ideal ⇒ $r_{oI}\to\infty$).
* $V_{out}$ is taken at the drain of M₂ (the high‑impedance node).

**DC bias.** With no gate currents, $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1$. Both devices are designed for saturation:

* M₁: $I_1=\tfrac12 k_n'(W/L)_1\,(V_{in}-V_{th1})^2(1+\lambda_1 V_X)$, requires $V_X\ge V_{in}-V_{th1}$.
* M₂: $V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_X=V_{ov2}$, so **$V_X\simeq V_{b1}-V_{ov2}$** (set by the bias, *independent* of $V_{out}$). M₂ needs $V_{out}-V_{b1}\ge V_{ov2}$.

Consequences: choosing $V_{b1}\ge V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$ keeps M₁ in saturation, and the minimum $V_{out}$ for full saturation is $\approx V_{ov1}+2V_{ov2}$ (the usual cascode head‑room penalty). The key DC benefit is that the drain of M₁ (node X) is held at a fixed low voltage, so M₁ sees almost no drain‑voltage swing from the output → its channel‑length modulation (and $g_{m}$ variation) is suppressed.

## 2. Small‑signal model

Let $g_{m1},r_{o1}$ be M₁’s and $g_{m2},r_{o2}$ M₂’s parameters. With $v_{in}=0$, M₁ (gate = source = 0) presents just $r_{o1}$ from X to ground.

**Input resistance:** $R_{in}=\infty$ (gate of M₁).

**Output resistance.** Look into the drain of M₂ with its source “degenerated” by $R_s=r_{o1}$ (gate AC‑grounded). The standard common‑gate result is

$$R_{\text{in,drain of M2}}=r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})\,r_{o1}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}.$$

This is in parallel with the load resistance $r_{oI}$:

$$\boxed{R_{out}=\big[r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\big]\;\|\;r_{oI}\;\approx\;g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\|\;r_{oI}}$$

**A_v = −gm₁·ro₁·[1 + (gm₂ + gmb₂)·ro₂] ≈ −(gm₁·ro₁)(gm₂·ro₂)**

Actually, since $I_1$ is a current source, $V_{out}$ is determined by the requirement that $M_2$ stays in saturation: $V_{out} > V_X + (V_{gs2} - V_{th})$.

This is where the "Cascode" nature of the circuit becomes apparent.
*   **Input Stage ($M_1$):** The input signal $v_{in}$ is applied to the gate of $M_1$. Since the source is at AC ground, $M_1$ operates as a Common Source amplifier. It converts the input voltage $v_{in}$ into an output current $i_{d1} \approx g_{m1} v_{in}$.

The total voltage gain $A_v$ is the product of the gains of the two stages (conceptually), or simply the transconductance of the input stage times the output resistance of the whole circuit.

*   **Signal Path:**
    1.  An input voltage change $\Delta v_{in}$ at the gate of $M_1$ modulates its drain current ($\Delta i_{d1} \approx g_{m1} \Delta v_{in}$).
    2.  Since $M_1$ and $M_2$ are in series, this change in current must flow through $M_2$ (KCL at node $X$). So, $\Delta i_{d2} \approx \Delta i_{d1}$.
